idiom_name: Enumerable#select/#filter with a block or &proc (Symbol#to_proc) + Enumerator::Lazy#filter for chains
implementation_notes: Filters are blocks: Enumerable#select (aliased filter) returns a new Array of the elements for which the block is truthy, and the block is itself a first-class Proc - a stored proc can be passed with &predicate and a no-argument predicate method with the Symbol#to_proc shorthand &:predicate?. The container-typed result is a one-line method returning a new instance of the same class: def filtered(&keep) = self.class.new(system_id, threats.select(&keep)). Enumerable#reject, #filter_map and parameterised lambdas cover the other criterion shapes, and Enumerator::Lazy#filter (from #lazy) keeps the chain from materialising intermediate arrays while evaluating values on demand. The classic filterer interface is unnecessary in a duck-typed language; a hand-written filterer object earns its place only when criteria must be inspectable data, which is closer to the Specification pattern.
pitfalls: Block versus lambda control flow: a proc passed as a block with return/break returns from the enclosing method (LocalJumpError or a surprising early exit); store criteria as lambdas or symbols instead.
Symbol#to_proc only works for public, zero-argument methods - a predicate with parameters needs a lambda, and a private predicate silently fails at call time.

Enumerable#select always walks the whole collection and builds an array, so for large or sparse filters the lazy form (#lazy.select) is the difference between a responsive program and a memory spike; the lazy enumerator is also single-shot once consumed.
A custom collection that includes Enumerable must implement each consistently - if it does not, every derived method (select, reject, filter_map) inherits the bug.
